### Example 1 · Page 88

Find the area enclosed by the curve $y=\cosh x+\tanh x$, the $y$-axis, the $x$-axis and the line $x=1$, correct to 3 significant figures.

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show solution</summary>

$$
\begin{aligned}
A&=\int_0^1(\cosh x+\tanh x)\,\mathrm dx\\
&=\Bigl[\sinh x+\ln(\cosh x)\Bigr]_0^1\\
&=\sinh1+\ln(\cosh1)-0\\
&=\boxed{1.61\ (3\text{ s.f.})}.
\end{aligned}
$$

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="int-p2-example-1"> Completed</label>
:::

::: {.study-card}
### Example 2 · Page 89

Find $\displaystyle\int_0^{\ln2}\operatorname{sech}x\,\mathrm dx$ correct to 3 significant figures.

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show solution</summary>

Using the definition $\operatorname{sech}x=\dfrac2{e^x+e^{-x}}$ and the substitution $u=e^x$, $\mathrm du=e^x\mathrm dx$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int\operatorname{sech}x\,\mathrm dx
&=\int\frac{2}{u+u^{-1}}\cdot\frac{\mathrm du}{u}
=2\int\frac{\mathrm du}{u^2+1}\\
&=2\tan^{-1}u+C
=2\tan^{-1}(e^x)+C.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore

$$
\int_0^{\ln2}\operatorname{sech}x\,\mathrm dx
=2\Bigl[\tan^{-1}(e^x)\Bigr]_0^{\ln2}
=2\left(\tan^{-1}2-\tan^{-1}1\right)
=\boxed{0.410\ (3\text{ s.f.})}.
$$

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="int-p2-example-2"> Completed</label>
:::

::: {.study-card}
### Example 3 · Page 92

Find $\displaystyle\int\frac{\mathrm dx}{\sqrt{x^2+x}}$ by completing the square, for $x>1$.

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show solution</summary>

Completing the square,

$$
x^2+x=\left(x+\frac12\right)^2-\frac14.
$$

Let $z=x+\frac12$ and $a=\frac12$. Then

$$
\int\frac{\mathrm dx}{\sqrt{x^2+x}}
=\int\frac{\mathrm dz}{\sqrt{z^2-a^2}}
=\cosh^{-1}\frac{z}{a}+C
=\boxed{\cosh^{-1}(2x+1)+C}.
$$

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="int-p2-example-3"> Completed</label>
:::

::: {.study-card}
### Example 4 · Page 92

Find $\displaystyle\int\frac{5\,\mathrm dx}{\sqrt{3x^2+12x+15}}$ by completing the square.

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show solution</summary>

Completing the square,

$$
3x^2+12x+15=3\bigl((x+2)^2+1\bigr).
$$

Therefore

$$
\int\frac{5\,\mathrm dx}{\sqrt{3x^2+12x+15}}
=\frac5{\sqrt3}\int\frac{\mathrm dx}{\sqrt{(x+2)^2+1}}
=\boxed{\frac5{\sqrt3}\sinh^{-1}(x+2)+C}.
$$

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="int-p2-example-4"> Completed</label>
:::

::: {.study-card}
### Example 5 · Page 94

Given that $I_n=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^nx\,\mathrm dx$, show that

$$
I_n=\frac{n-1}{n}I_{n-2}
$$

and hence evaluate $I_5$.

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show solution</summary>

Write $\sin^nx=\sin^{n-1}x\sin x$ and integrate by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}
I_n&=\Bigl[-\cos x\sin^{n-1}x\Bigr]_0^{\pi/2}
+(n-1)\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^2x\sin^{n-2}x\,\mathrm dx\\
&=0+(n-1)\int_0^{\pi/2}(1-\sin^2x)\sin^{n-2}x\,\mathrm dx\\
&=(n-1)I_{n-2}-(n-1)I_n.
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence

$$
nI_n=(n-1)I_{n-2}
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\boxed{I_n=\frac{n-1}{n}I_{n-2}}.
$$

Using $I_1=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin x\,\mathrm dx=1$,

$$
I_5=\frac45\cdot\frac23\cdot I_1
=\frac45\cdot\frac23
=\boxed{\frac8{15}}.
$$

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="int-p2-example-5"> Completed</label>
:::

::: {.study-card}
### Example 6 · Page 95

**(a)** Find $\displaystyle\int_0^1e^{-x}\,\mathrm dx$.

**(b)** Find a reduction formula for the integral $\displaystyle I_n=\int_0^1e^{-x}(1-x)^n\,\mathrm dx$.

**(c)** Hence find $\displaystyle\int_0^1e^{-x}(1-x)^2\,\mathrm dx$.

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show solution</summary>

**(a)**

$$
\int_0^1e^{-x}\,\mathrm dx=\Bigl[-e^{-x}\Bigr]_0^1=\boxed{1-\frac1e}.
$$

**(b)** Integrating by parts with $u=(1-x)^n$, $\mathrm dv=e^{-x}\mathrm dx$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
I_n&=\Bigl[-e^{-x}(1-x)^n\Bigr]_0^1-n\int_0^1e^{-x}(1-x)^{n-1}\,\mathrm dx\\
&=1-nI_{n-1}.
\end{aligned}
$$

So

$$
\boxed{I_n=1-nI_{n-1}}.
$$

**(c)** Using the reduction formula repeatedly:

$$
I_2=1-2I_1=1-2(1-I_0)=1-2\left(1-\left(1-\frac1e\right)\right)
=1-2\cdot\frac1e
=\boxed{1-\frac2e}.
$$

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="int-p2-example-6"> Completed</label>
:::

::: {.study-card}
### Example 7 · Page 95

Given that $I_n=\displaystyle\int_0^1(1-x)^ne^{-x}\,\mathrm dx$, find a reduction formula for $I_n$ by splitting $(1-x)^n$ into $(1-x)^{n-1}(1-x)$.

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show solution</summary>

Write

$$
I_n=\int_0^1(1-x)^{n-1}(1-x)e^{-x}\,\mathrm dx.
$$

Using integration by parts with $u=(1-x)^n$, $\mathrm dv=e^{-x}\mathrm dx$,

$$
I_n=\Bigl[-e^{-x}(1-x)^n\Bigr]_0^1
-n\int_0^1e^{-x}(1-x)^{n-1}\,\mathrm dx.
$$

Hence

$$
\boxed{I_n=1-nI_{n-1}}.
$$

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="int-p2-example-7"> Completed</label>
:::

::: {.study-card}
### Example 8 · Page 96

Find $\dfrac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\left(\tan x\sec^nx\right)$ in terms of $\sec x$. Hence find a reduction formula for $\displaystyle I_n=\int_0^{\pi/4}\sec^nx\,\mathrm dx$.

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show solution</summary>

Using the product rule,

$$
\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\left(\tan x\sec^nx\right)
=\sec^{n+2}x+n\sec^nx\tan^2x
=(n+1)\sec^{n+2}x-n\sec^nx.
$$

Integrating from $0$ to $\pi/4$,

$$
\Bigl[\tan x\sec^nx\Bigr]_0^{\pi/4}
=(n+1)I_{n+2}-nI_n.
$$

At $x=\pi/4$, $\tan x=1$ and $\sec x=\sqrt2$, so the left-hand side is $(\sqrt2)^n=2^{n/2}$. Hence

$$
2^{n/2}=(n+1)I_{n+2}-nI_n,
$$

giving

$$
\boxed{I_{n+2}=\frac{2^{n/2}+nI_n}{n+1}}.
$$

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="int-p2-example-8"> Completed</label>
:::

::: {.study-card}
### Example 9 · Page 97

Find the area under the curve $y=1+x^2$ between $x=1$ and $x=2$ by using rectangles of width $\frac15$ that underestimate the area. Find the area exactly by integrating, and give the percentage error of the approximation correct to 1 significant figure.

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show solution</summary>

Using five rectangles of width $\frac15$ that underestimate the area (using left endpoints $1.0,1.2,1.4,1.6,1.8$):

$$
A\approx\frac15\Bigl[(1^2+1)+(1.2^2+1)+(1.4^2+1)+(1.6^2+1)+(1.8^2+1)\Bigr]
=3.04.
$$

The exact area is

$$
\int_1^2(1+x^2)\,\mathrm dx
=\Bigl[x+\frac{x^3}{3}\Bigr]_1^2
=2+\frac83-1-\frac13
=\frac{10}{3}\approx3.333.
$$

The percentage error is

$$
\frac{3.04-3.333}{3.333}\times100\approx\boxed{-9\%\ (1\text{ s.f.})}.
$$

(Using right-endpoint rectangles gives $3.64$, an overestimate of $+9\%$; the average gives an estimate with error about $+0.2\%$.)

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="int-p2-example-9"> Completed</label>
:::

### Example 10 · Page 99

Show that

$$
\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac1{n}\left(1+\frac{r}{n}\right)^{-1}\approx\int_0^1\frac{\mathrm dx}{1+x},
$$

with the approximation improving as $n$ increases.

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show solution</summary>

Taking $n$ rectangles of width $\frac1n$ under the curve $y=\frac1{1+x}$ from $x=0$ to $x=1$ (using the right endpoints $x=\frac rn$):

$$
\text{sum of areas}
=\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac1n\cdot\frac1{1+\frac rn}.
$$

As $n\to\infty$, the rectangles fit the curve more closely, so

$$
\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac1n\left(1+\frac rn\right)^{-1}
\longrightarrow
\int_0^1\frac{\mathrm dx}{1+x}
=\Bigl[\ln(1+x)\Bigr]_0^1
=\ln2.
$$

Hence

$$
\boxed{\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac1{n}\left(1+\frac{r}{n}\right)^{-1}\approx\ln2},
$$

with the approximation improving as $n$ increases.

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="int-p2-example-10"> Completed</label>
:::

::: {.study-card}
### Example 11 · Page 102

Find the length of the curve given by $x=\cos t$, $y=\sin t$ from $t=0$ to $t=\pi/2$.

**(a)** by seeing this as an arc of a circle;

**(b)** by using the parametric form for arc length.

Check that both methods give the same answer.

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show solution</summary>

**(a)** Eliminating $t$ gives $x^2+y^2=1$. The required arc is the quarter-circle from $(1,0)$ to $(0,1)$, whose length is

$$
\frac14\cdot2\pi=\boxed{\frac{\pi}{2}}.
$$

**(b)** Using

$$
s=\int_0^{\pi/2}\sqrt{\left(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}\right)^2}\,\mathrm dt,
$$

with $\dfrac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=-\sin t$, $\dfrac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=\cos t$,

$$
s=\int_0^{\pi/2}\sqrt{\sin^2t+\cos^2t}\,\mathrm dt
=\int_0^{\pi/2}1\,\mathrm dt
=\boxed{\frac{\pi}{2}}.
$$

Both methods agree.

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="int-p2-example-11"> Completed</label>
:::

### Example 12 · Page 103

**(a)** Find the derivative of $\ln\left(x+\sqrt{x^2+1}\right)+x\sqrt{x^2+1}$ and hence find $\displaystyle\int\sqrt{1+x^2}\,\mathrm dx$.

**(b)** Find the length of the spiral defined by $r=\theta$ for $0\leqslant\theta\leqslant\pi/2$.

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show solution</summary>

**(a)** Differentiating $\ln\left(x+\sqrt{x^2+1}\right)$ using the chain rule,

$$
\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\ln\left(x+\sqrt{x^2+1}\right)
=\frac{1+\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+1}}}{x+\sqrt{x^2+1}}
=\frac1{\sqrt{x^2+1}}.
$$

Differentiating $x\sqrt{x^2+1}$ by the product rule,

$$
\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\left(x\sqrt{x^2+1}\right)
=\sqrt{x^2+1}+\frac{x^2}{\sqrt{x^2+1}}
=\frac{2x^2+1}{\sqrt{x^2+1}}.
$$

Adding the two derivatives,

$$
\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\left(\ln\left(x+\sqrt{x^2+1}\right)+x\sqrt{x^2+1}\right)
=\frac{2x^2+2}{\sqrt{x^2+1}}
=2\sqrt{x^2+1}.
$$

Hence

$$
\int\sqrt{1+x^2}\,\mathrm dx
=\boxed{\frac12\left(\ln\left(x+\sqrt{x^2+1}\right)+x\sqrt{x^2+1}\right)+C}.
$$

**(b)** For $r=\theta$, using the polar arc-length formula,

$$
s=\int_0^{\pi/2}\sqrt{r^2+\left(\frac{\mathrm dr}{\mathrm d\theta}\right)^2}\,\mathrm d\theta
=\int_0^{\pi/2}\sqrt{\theta^2+1}\,\mathrm d\theta
\approx2.30.
$$

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="int-p2-example-12"> Completed</label>
:::

::: {.study-card}
### Example 13 · Page 105

Find the surface area of revolution formed by rotating the line $y=x$ through $2\pi$ about the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=1$.

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show solution</summary>

Using

$$
A=2\pi\int_0^1 y\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\right)^2}\,\mathrm dx,
$$

with $y=x$ and $\dfrac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=1$,

$$
A=2\pi\int_0^1 x\sqrt2\,\mathrm dx
=2\pi\sqrt2\cdot\frac12
=\boxed{\pi\sqrt2}.
$$

This is the curved surface area of a cone of slant height $\sqrt2$ and base radius $1$: $A=\pi r l=\pi\sqrt2$.

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="int-p2-example-13"> Completed</label>
:::

::: {.study-card}
### Example 14 · Page 105

Find the surface area of a sphere by rotating the top half of the circle $x^2+y^2=a^2$ through $360^\circ$ about the $x$-axis.

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show solution</summary>

The top half is $y=\sqrt{a^2-x^2}$, and

$$
\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=-\frac{x}{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}}.
$$

Therefore

$$
\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\right)^2}
=\sqrt{1+\frac{x^2}{a^2-x^2}}
=\frac{a}{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}}.
$$

So

$$
A=2\pi\int_{-a}^{a}\sqrt{a^2-x^2}\cdot\frac{a}{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}}\,\mathrm dx
=2\pi\int_{-a}^{a}a\,\mathrm dx
=2\pi a(2a)
=\boxed{4\pi a^2}.
$$

This agrees with the standard formula for the surface area of a sphere.

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="int-p2-example-14"> Completed</label>
:::

::: {.study-card}
### Example 15 · Page 106

The curve $C$ is defined by $x=t^2$, $y=t-\frac13t^3$. Find the surface area created when the portion of the curve from $t=0$ to $t=1$ is rotated through $360^\circ$ about the $x$-axis.

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show solution</summary>

Using

$$
A=2\pi\int_{t_1}^{t_2}y\sqrt{\left(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}\right)^2}\,\mathrm dt,
$$

with

$$
\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=2t,\qquad
\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=1-t^2,
$$

we have

$$
\sqrt{(2t)^2+(1-t^2)^2}=t^2+1.
$$

Therefore

$$
A=2\pi\int_0^1\left(t-\frac13t^3\right)(t^2+1)\,\mathrm dt
=2\pi\int_0^1\left(t^3+t-\frac13t^5-\frac13t^3\right)\mathrm dt.
$$

Evaluating,

$$
A=2\pi\left[\frac{t^4}{4}+\frac{t^2}{2}-\frac{t^6}{18}-\frac{t^4}{12}\right]_0^1
=2\pi\left(\frac14+\frac12-\frac1{18}-\frac1{12}\right).
$$

So

$$
A=2\pi\left(\frac{9+18-2-3}{36}\right)
=2\pi\cdot\frac{22}{36}
=\boxed{\frac{11\pi}{9}}.
$$

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="int-p2-example-15"> Completed</label>
:::
